newsitem.title: UK: Coffee, copper prices punch higher.
newsitem.headline: Coffee, copper prices punch higher.

text.p: Coffee prices launched a fresh assault towards the key $1,600 a tonne level on Tuesday as investment funds expanded their holdings.
But arbitrage selling dented the rise, fuelled by supply concerns in Brazil, and London's benchmark March robusta contract stalled at an intraday $1,580.
It ended the day at an even lower $1,557, up $27.
But traders expected prices to keep bubbling after a 30-percent hike since the beginning of the year and amid signs of a rise in industry costs translating into higher prices on supermarket shelves.

"The question is how long this (rally) is going to go on. It seems the speculators have got a new toy to play with and they are playing to the fullest extent and there's no reason not to push the market further," one robusta trader said.
Elsewhere in commodity markets, copper flipped back above $2,200 in a late rally, brushing aside a rise in London Metal Exchange stocks and more freely available nearby material.
Three months delivery ended at $2,204 a tonne, gaining a respectable $27 by the end of trading on the exchange.
But Monday's star performers nickel and zinc opted for consolidation, with nickel waving goodbye to a 4-1/2 month high of $7,740 a tonne as it ended at $7,675. Aluminium also eased.
Gold fixed $2 higher at $345.70 an ounce but failed to excite enough interest to chase $350 as prices continued to languish at 3-1/2 year lows, traders said.

"New York tried to push it up to $347 a couple of times, but it came right back down again. I think the market was just fed up with it," said a dealer. "It had to break $347 to get anywhere higher, but it just looks so unattractive."

The only precious metal that bucked the trend was palladium which popped up to fix a $128.00/ounce, the highest level in six months, amid delays in contract talks between major producer Russia and Japan, which uses the metal in auto exhaust systems.
Traders expected little direction from the U.S. Federal Reserve's two-day meeting which starts on Tuesday, saying interest rates were unlikely to change with tame inflation.
Cocoa and sugar performed poorly. Cocoa longs were getting increasingly frustrated by the market's marked reluctance to push higher. The key May contract ended 10 stg lower in London at 923.
Wheat also shared cocoa's fate, staying in the doldrums with no signs of a change in ample world-wide supplies in the immediate future.
By mid-morning, Chicago March wheat had traded as low as five cents a bushel down at $3.56-1/2, while soybean futures were up as on lack of aggressive fund liquidation.
